profile.summary: scCello is a transcriptome foundation model for single-cell RNA-seq data. It reads a cell as a list of genes ordered by expression and outputs a cell representation (and masked-gene predictions). During pre-training it also uses each cell's cell-type label and the cell ontology graph, so that cells of the same or related types end up close together.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: Overview; arXiv 2408.12373 Abstract and Section 2.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scCello is a stack of transformer encoder layers. Each cell's genes are normalised and ranked by expression (rank value encoding, taken from Geneformer) and fed in as a sequence of gene tokens. Pre-training minimises four losses together: masked gene prediction as in BERT, an intra-cellular cell-type coherence loss that pulls cells of the same type together, an inter-cellular relational alignment loss that uses similarities between cell types computed on the cell ontology graph, and a regularisation term.
sections.source_locator: arXiv 2408.12373 Sections 2.1 to 2.5; Appendix D

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README names one pre-trained checkpoint on Hugging Face, katarinayuan/scCello-zeroshot. The README loads the same checkpoint both for zero-shot use and, with a classification head, for linear probing. The checkpoint repository holds config.json and pytorch_model.bin and no model card. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision, and the repository commit used to run it.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Model Checkpoints; Hugging Face API response

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: The authors evaluate scCello on cell type clustering and batch integration, cell type classification, classification of novel cell types, marker gene prediction and cancer drug response prediction. The repository has one script per task.

profile.summary: scPRINT is a transformer model for single-cell RNA-seq data, built mainly to infer gene networks. It takes the raw counts of a cell and can, without fine-tuning, denoise expression, produce a cell embedding, predict labels such as cell type, disease, sequencer, sex and ethnicity, and output a cell-specific gene network.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each gene in a cell is represented by the sum of three embeddings: its identity, its expression and its genomic location. The identity embedding is the ESM2 protein embedding of the gene's most common protein product. The paper says these gene embeddings can be frozen during training or used only for initialisation. A bidirectional transformer encodes the cell. Pre-training adds three losses together: denoising (recover a profile from a downsampled one), bottleneck learning (regenerate the expression profile from the cell embedding alone) and hierarchical label prediction. scPRINT generates a gene network by selecting and combining attention heads into a gene by gene matrix.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results: scPRINT; Fig. 1 caption

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The Hugging Face repository jkobject/scPRINT holds the checkpoints small-v1, small-v2, medium-v1, medium-v1.5 and large-v1, plus cell-transformer, esm-ft and many run-ID checkpoints under other_ckpts. The README uses medium-v1.5 in its examples. To reproduce the paper the README asks for version tag 1.6.4. The authors have since released scPRINT-2 in a separate repository. A result should name the checkpoint file, the Hugging Face revision and the package version.

profile.summary: LangCell is a single-cell language model trained on pairs of single-cell transcriptomes and text descriptions of cell identity. It places cells and text in one shared feature space, so it can annotate cell types zero-shot by matching a cell against text descriptions of candidate types, as well as after few-shot training or fine-tuning.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Checkpoint; arXiv Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LangCell has a cell encoder and a text encoder. The cell encoder is initialised from a pre-trained Geneformer and takes Geneformer-style tokenised cells, with a [CLS] token whose embedding is projected into the shared space. The text encoder is initialised from PubMedBERT and has a cross-attention mode that scores whether a cell and a text match. Pre-training jointly optimises four losses: masked gene modelling, cell-cell contrastive learning, cell-text contrastive learning and cell-text matching. It runs in two stages: first the cell encoder alone with the first two losses, then all four.
sections.source_locator: arXiv Sections 3 and 4.1; README.md: Checkpoint

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint is distributed as a Google Drive folder, split into five modules: text_bert, cell_bert, text_proj, cell_proj and ctm_head. cell_bert is a standard Hugging Face BertModel and can be used alone as LangCell-CE. The checkpoint has no version label or hash in the README, so a result should name the repository commit and the date the checkpoint was downloaded.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Checkpoint; Usage

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Cell identity understanding, mainly cell type annotation: zero-shot from text descriptions, few-shot, and fine-tuning of the cell encoder. Text descriptions of new cell types can be written following the OBO Foundry examples the authors provide.

profile.summary: UCE (Universal Cell Embeddings) is a foundation model that maps single-cell RNA-seq profiles from any tissue or species into one shared embedding space. It takes raw counts plus protein language model embeddings of the genes, and outputs a cell embedding without any labelling, training or fine-tuning on the new dataset.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Abstract and Fig. 1 legend; README.md: Output

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: For each cell UCE draws a weighted sample of expressed genes (1,024 genes, with replacement). Each gene is represented by the ESM2 embedding of its protein product, so any protein-coding gene from any species can be represented from sequence. Genes are sorted by genomic location and grouped by chromosome with start and end tokens, then passed through a transformer. The cell embedding is the final-layer output of a CLS token. Training masks some expressed genes and asks a network, given the cell embedding and a gene's protein embedding, whether that gene was expressed.
sections.source_locator: Paper Fig. 1 legend; Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained models are on Figshare: 4layer_model.torch, which the script uses by default, and 33l_8ep_1024t_1280.torch, the 33-layer model from the paper. Embeddings from the two are not compatible with each other. Figshare article 24320806 is at version 5. A result should name the model file, the Figshare version and the repository commit.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Embedding a new dataset, Data; Figshare API response

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Zero-shot embedding of new single-cell datasets, for example to build integrated atlases or to transfer a cell type classifier to a new dataset. The authors used it to build the Integrated Mega-scale Atlas of 36 million cells.
sections.source_locator: Paper Abstract and Discussion

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Zero-shot foundation model for single-cell gene expression that produces cell embeddings.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Transformer over gene tokens built from ESM2 protein embeddings, ordered by chromosome and genomic position, with a CLS token for the cell embedding. The paper's model has 33 layers; a 4-layer model is also released.

strengths.text: Zero-shot: new datasets are embedded without labels, training or fine-tuning.
Genes are represented by protein embeddings, so the authors state any protein-coding gene from any species can be represented, including species not in the training data.
Code and weights carry permissive licences (MIT and CC BY 4.0), and the embedding script downloads the default model files itself.

limitations.text: Only 1,024 genes are sampled per cell, fewer than some cells express; the authors tie this to the quadratic cost of attention.
The 4-layer and 33-layer models give incompatible embeddings, and the paper's datasets were embedded with the 33-layer model.
Large downloads: the 33-layer model file is 5,686,283,829 bytes and the protein embeddings archive 2,735,410,523 bytes. The README sizes batches for an 80GB GPU.
Gene names must be symbols, not Ensembl IDs.

profile.summary: CellPLM is a pre-trained transformer for single-cell transcriptomics that treats each cell as a token and a tissue (a set of cells) as a sentence, so it can model relations between cells. It takes gene expression for a set of cells and outputs cell embeddings; the repository's tutorials apply it to cell embedding, cell type annotation and spatial imputation.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Instead of treating genes as tokens, CellPLM treats cells as tokens and tissues as sentences. It is pre-trained on single-cell and spatially resolved transcriptomic data so that it learns cell-cell relations, and it uses a Gaussian mixture prior on the latent space as an extra inductive bias. The shipped configuration names a flowformer encoder (4 layers, hidden size 1024), a gmvae latent module with 512 dimensions and 16 clusters, and a decoder module named nbmlp, trained with masking of 75% of nodes and 25% of features.

profile.summary: GenePT builds gene and cell embeddings from text instead of training on expression data. Each gene's NCBI summary is embedded with an OpenAI text embedding model; a cell embedding is then either the expression-weighted average of its gene embeddings (GenePT-w) or the text embedding of the cell's gene names ordered by expression (GenePT-s). The embeddings feed gene-level and cell-level tasks such as gene property and cell type classification.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: What is GenePT?; paper Methods 3.1

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: About 33,000 genes were taken from the scGPT and Geneformer vocabularies and genes in the downstream datasets. Each gene's NCBI summary was embedded with text-embedding-ada-002, giving a 1,536-dimensional gene vector. For cells, counts are normalised to 10,000 per cell and log(1 + x) transformed. GenePT-w takes the expression-weighted average of the gene vectors and scales it to unit length. GenePT-s writes the expressed gene names in descending order of expression as a sentence and embeds that sentence. No model is trained on expression data.

sections.body: The released artefact is a set of precomputed gene embeddings on Zenodo (record 10833191, one zip file). In March 2024 the authors added embeddings that include UniProt protein summaries and embeddings from the newer text-embedding-3-large model, alongside the original text-embedding-ada-002 ones. A result should state which summary file and which embedding model were used, since GenePT-w results depend on that choice.

profile.summary: scGPT-spatial is a foundation model for spatial transcriptomics, made by continuing the pre-training of the scGPT single-cell model on 30 million spatial profiles. It takes spatial transcriptomic data from imaging or sequencing protocols (Visium, Visium HD, Xenium, MERFISH) and outputs zero-shot cell or spot embeddings for multi-slide and multi-modal integration; the authors report that the model also supports cell-type deconvolution and missing gene imputation.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scGPT-spatial starts from the published scGPT model and continues pre-training on the SpatialHuman30M corpus. It adds a Mixture of Experts decoder that routes each sample to protocol-aware decoding of gene expression, samples training data in a spatially aware way, and uses a neighbourhood-based reconstruction objective to capture which cell states co-locate in tissue. At inference, embed_data returns an embedding per cell or spot.

profile.summary: Nicheformer is a transformer foundation model trained on both dissociated single-cell and image-based spatial transcriptomics from human and mouse. It turns each cell's expression into a ranked sequence of gene tokens, with tokens for species, modality and assay, and outputs a 512-dimensional cell embedding that can be fine-tuned or linearly probed to predict spatial labels and spatial composition.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Genes from human and mouse are merged into one vocabulary of 20,310 gene tokens, covering orthologous protein-coding genes and species-specific ones. Each cell's expression vector becomes a sequence of gene tokens ranked by expression, plus metadata tokens. A 12-layer transformer encoder with 16 attention heads, a feed-forward size of 1,024 and a 1,500-token context is pre-trained to predict masked tokens. The cell embedding is an aggregate of the gene token outputs. Spatial coordinates are not used in pre-training.

profile.summary: scELMo uses large language models to describe genes (or other features and cell metadata) in text and to embed those descriptions, then combines the embeddings with single-cell expression data to make cell embeddings. Without training a new model the cell embeddings support clustering, batch effect correction and cell type annotation; a small fine-tuned adaptor handles harder tasks such as perturbation analysis.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Feature information (for example genes or proteins) is turned into text, either from a database such as NCBI or as a summary written by an LLM, and the text is embedded with an LLM. A cell's embedding combines these feature embeddings with its expression profile. Unlike GenePT's arithmetic average, scELMo also offers a weighted average that uses expression levels as weights. In the fine-tuning framework, a light model (an adaptor) is trained on the gene embeddings and expression profiles.

profile.summary: BACPI predicts how a small molecule and a protein relate, from sequence alone. It takes the SMILES string of a compound and the amino acid sequence of a protein, and returns either a binary interaction label or a continuous binding affinity value, depending on which of the two tasks it is trained for. A graph attention network encodes the compound, a convolutional network encodes the protein, and a bi-directional attention module combines the two representations before the prediction layer.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstractText, Results; README.md: Example usage

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The compound is turned into a molecular graph with RDKit and a 1024-bit Morgan fingerprint, and the protein sequence is cut into overlapping 3-mers that are mapped to learned embeddings. Atom embeddings pass through several graph attention heads; the protein embeddings pass through a stack of convolutional layers. A bi-directional attention block then scores every atom against every residue, pools both sides with the resulting attention weights, and feeds the combined compound and protein vectors to the output layer. The output layer has one unit for the affinity task and two for the interaction task, trained with mean squared error and cross entropy respectively.

sections.title: What it is trained and evaluated on
sections.body: The repository ships its own data. Four affinity archives, named Ki, IC50, Kd and EC50, are unpacked by a preparation script that reads BindingDB column names and keeps the ligand SMILES, the target chain sequence and the chosen measure. Two interaction sets, human and celegans, are shipped as plain train and test text files. The abstract states that three CPI datasets and four binding affinity datasets were used in the paper's experiments, so one of the paper's CPI datasets is not in the repository files listed here.

profile.summary: MixingDTA predicts drug-target affinity: given a drug SMILES string and a protein sequence, it returns a continuous affinity value. It does not learn its own sequence representations. Instead it takes embeddings from two pretrained language models, MolFormer for the molecule and ESM3-open for the protein, and feeds them to a trained aggregation network called MEETA. A data augmentation step called GBA-Mixup then builds extra training pairs by interpolating the embeddings of neighbouring drugs and proteins, which is aimed at sparse regions of affinity space and at unseen drugs or proteins.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Figure 1 caption; README.md: Abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MEETA, the backbone, replaces the usual multi-head attention between drug and protein tokens with attention-free aggregation, which the authors say has linear rather than quadratic cost in sequence length and therefore lets them keep full drug and protein sequences instead of truncating them. The code implements this as a cross_AFT block with query, key and value projections in both directions, drug against protein and protein against drug, followed by a regression head that outputs a single value. The drug embeddings come from MolFormer-XL and the protein embeddings from ESM3-open with 1.4B parameters; everything in MEETA after those two encoders is trained. GBA-Mixup then samples a mixing ratio from a Beta distribution and interpolates the embeddings and labels of neighbouring drug-target pairs, where neighbours are defined by six perspectives. A meta-predictor finally combines the embeddings of the six encoders trained on those perspectives.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Introduction, Methods 2.2 and 2.3, Figure 1 caption; model.py: cross_AFT, Regress, DTA; config.py: configuration; README.md: etc

sections.title: Training and the six perspectives
sections.body: Training runs in two stages. In the first, the MEETA model is trained once for each of six cases, which the configuration file names none, all pair, drug, protein, drug and protein, and reversed, and which differ in how neighbouring pairs are connected and whether mixup is applied. In the second stage the six trained encoders are combined by a meta-predictor. The defaults in the configuration are 500 epochs, batch size 64, AdamW with a learning rate of 5e-5, an embedding width of 256 and five splits. The datasets are DAVIS, KIBA, BindingDB_Kd and PDBbind_Refined, the first three taken from TDC and shipped in the repository as pickle files already split for five-fold cross validation. The paper reports five-fold cross validation on DAVIS and KIBA with a train, validation and test ratio of 6:2:2, and full strings without truncation.

profile.summary: HyCell is a compact single-cell embedding model. It maps the raw counts of one human cell to a 512-dimensional embedding that is used as a frozen representation for clustering, integration across batches, annotation transfer and comparison of cell states; its decoder turns embeddings back into expected gene expression.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A cell is an unordered set of gene tokens with no positional encoding. Each expressed gene contributes a learned gene embedding plus a small network applied to its log1p counts per 10,000. Up to 818 expressed genes enter, with measured zeros numbering a quarter of the expressed genes and a [CLS] token, at most 1,024 tokens. A six-layer transformer (width 256, four heads, SwiGLU) encodes the set and a linear projection of the final [CLS] state is the embedding. In training, a negative-binomial count decoder conditioned on learned dataset and donor codes reconstructs the profile, and a donor discriminator is trained against the encoder. The README says the 818 genes are the highest by value; the report says genes are sampled with probability increasing in expression when a cell expresses more. The sources do not reconcile the two.
sections.source_locator: Package README: Method; technical report Section 2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One checkpoint, hycell-16m version 0.1.0, ships inside the package (64 MB) with a sidecar recording its configuration and the SHA-256 of the weights; hycell info --verify checks it. The README states that on a CUDA GPU with flash-attn the package reproduces the report's embeddings bit for bit, and that PyTorch attention agrees up to rounding. A result should name hycell-16m, package version 0.1.0 and the weights hash.
sections.source_locator: weights.json; package README: Install, Reproducibility

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Frozen embeddings for clustering, batch integration, annotation transfer and comparing cells across donors and studies; decoding embeddings to expression; fine-tuning into a cell type annotator. The README advises reading donor-level properties such as sex or disease state from embeddings averaged per donor or sample.
sections.source_locator: Package README: Embed, Decode, Fine-tune

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Single-cell embedding model with a count decoder, used as a frozen encoder.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Set transformer: 6 layers, width 256, 4 heads, SwiGLU feed-forward 704, no positional encoding; 512-d embedding from the [CLS] state; negative-binomial decoder with 64-d dataset and donor codes; donor discriminator in training only.

facts.label: Inputs

facts.label: Outputs

facts.label: Parameters

profile.summary: MIST (Metabolite Inference with Spectrum Transformers) is a neural network for untargeted metabolomics. It takes a tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of an unknown small molecule, labels each peak with a chemical formula, and predicts a molecular fingerprint. A second, contrastively trained model embeds spectra so that candidate structures from a reference list can be ranked for annotation.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Nature Machine Intelligence abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each MS/MS peak is assigned a candidate chemical formula (subformula labelling), and a transformer encodes the set of formula-labelled peaks rather than a binned spectrum. The paper describes encoding peaks by their formula, implicitly featurising pairwise neutral losses, and training the network to also predict substructure fragments (the training command shows an auxiliary MAGMa loss). The fingerprint model predicts a 4096-bit Morgan fingerprint in the README example. A contrastive model is then trained on top of the fingerprint model with decoy molecules, so that spectra and candidate molecules can be compared by distance. Training also uses simulated spectra from a separate forward model (ICEBERG, from the ms-pred repository) as data augmentation.
sections.source_locator: README.md: introduction, Training models, Change log; article abstract

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The default branch, main_v2, is an updated version of MIST, not the code of the published paper. Its change log lists model changes (internal subformula labelling, sinusoidal formula embeddings, a simplified architecture, Adam instead of RAdam, augmentation moved to the external ms-pred repository) and analysis changes (worst-case tie handling in retrieval, no ensembles). The quickstart downloads two pretrained checkpoints trained on the public canopus_train (NPLIB1) data: mist_fp_canopus_pretrain.ckpt and mist_contrastive_canopus_pretrain.ckpt, from Zenodo record 8316682. That record is titled v2.0.0, but its related identifier points to the v1.0.1 tag, and the record is not flagged as the last version; the sources do not explain this. A result should name the branch or commit, the checkpoint file, and the split file used.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Update, Change log; quickstart/00_download_models.sh; Zenodo record metadata

sections.title: Use in benchmarks
sections.body: The MSAlign benchmark paper (an existing source on this record) ran MIST as a retrieval baseline and describes it as pretraining with fingerprint prediction, fine-tuning with contrastive learning, and augmenting data with a forward model.
sections.source_locator: MSAlign arXiv 2605.19752v2, Section 5.1 Baselines

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised neural network that maps MS/MS spectra to molecular fingerprints, plus a contrastive model for spectrum embedding and candidate retrieval.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Transformer over formula-labelled peaks. In the updated branch all inputs are concatenated once, passed through the transformer, pooled and run through an MLP.

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: MS/MS spectra (an MGF file or .ms files) with a labels table that includes each spectrum's chemical formula; subformula assignments are computed from the spectra. Retrieval also needs a list of candidate SMILES.

facts.label: Outputs
facts.value: Predicted fingerprints, dense spectrum embeddings, and ranked candidate molecules from a reference list.

facts.label: Parameters
facts.value: Not reported in the sources read. The README training example uses hidden size 256, 2 peak attention layers and 4 refine layers.

facts.label: Training data
facts.value: The released checkpoints are trained on canopus_train (renamed NPLIB1), public GNPS data. The paper's main benchmarks used csi2022, which includes NIST spectra and cannot be redistributed. Training adds simulated spectra from a forward model run on unpaired molecule libraries.

facts.label: Known versions
facts.value: The published (paper) version and the updated main_v2 branch; Zenodo record 8316682 is titled v2.0.0. Two released checkpoints: mist_fp_canopus_pretrain.ckpt (fingerprint) and mist_contrastive_canopus_pretrain.ckpt (contrastive). The related MIST-CF predicts precursor formulae and is a separate repository.

facts.label: Training cutoff
facts.value: Not stated. The Zenodo record with the checkpoints was published on 2023-09-07.

facts.label: Context limits
facts.value: Not stated as a model limit. The quickstart keeps up to 50 candidate formulae when it labels subformulae, which is a preprocessing setting.

facts.label: Weights licence
facts.value: other-open, as declared on the Zenodo record that holds the checkpoints; the exact terms are not given in the saved record.

facts.label: Code licence
facts.value: MIT, per the repository LICENSE.md.

facts.label: Access
facts.value: Code: https://github.com/samgoldman97/mist (default branch main_v2). Checkpoints: Zenodo record 8316682 (https://zenodo.org/records/8316682). Paper: https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-023-00708-3.

strengths.text: Pretrained checkpoints and a quickstart that runs fingerprint prediction, embedding and retrieval on a bundled example are provided.
Code is MIT-licensed and the repository includes the configs and scripts used for the paper experiments.
The authors report that MIST did better than standard neural architectures and a kernel method on fingerprint prediction for over 70% of metabolite standards (the authors' claim).

The main benchmark dataset (csi2022, with NIST) cannot be redistributed, so some paper comparisons cannot be rerun.
The environment targets CUDA 11.1 and was tested on Ubuntu 20.04; the retrieval database for training is not in the download and is larger than 5 GB.

profile.summary: Novae is a graph-based foundation model for spatial transcriptomics. It takes a spatial dataset at single-cell or spot resolution, builds a graph of neighbouring cells, and outputs a representation of each cell in its spatial context, which is used to assign spatial domains zero-shot across gene panels, tissues and technologies, with batch-effect correction built in.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Novae computes the spatial neighbours of each cell and learns cell representations with self-supervision on these graphs, a method adapted from SwAV. Representations are assigned to learned prototypes, which the documentation describes as elementary spatial domains; batch information is used only during training. The default human model's configuration sets 10 layers, 16 heads, hidden size 128, embedding size 512, output size 64 and 512 prototypes, with neighbourhood views of 2 hops.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Overview and Usage; docs/faq.md; novae-human-0 config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Pretrained models on Hugging Face: novae-human-0 (the default for human tissues), novae-mouse-0 and novae-brain-0, each with 32,041,793 parameters, all created on 10 September 2024; and novae-scConcept-multi-species, with 3,124,983 parameters, created on 19 June 2026. The README announces a new improved model with a tutorial at a novae_scConcept page; it does not name the Hugging Face repository. A novae-test repository also exists. A result should name the model repository, its revision and the novae package version.
sections.source_locator: Hugging Face API responses; README.md: Recent updates

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Zero-shot or fine-tuned spatial domain assignment, batch-effect correction across slides, analysis of spatially variable genes and pathways, and architecture analysis of tissue slides; an optional multimodal mode uses H&E image embeddings.
sections.source_locator: README.md; docs/faq.md

profile.summary: MassFormer predicts the tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of a small molecule from its structure. It takes a molecule (as SMILES) plus spectrum metadata such as precursor adduct and collision energy, and outputs a binned spectrum. Predicted spectra can be used to identify compounds by comparing them with measured spectra.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MassFormer adapts the Graphormer graph transformer. Node and edge embeddings are taken from the molecular graph, the graph transformer models relationships between all atoms, and a readout gives one embedding for the molecule. This embedding is combined with metadata (precursor adduct, collision energy) and passed to an MLP that outputs a binned spectrum. The transformer and input embeddings are initialised from a Graphormer model pre-trained on PCQM4Mv2 (about 4 million molecular graphs with simulated HOMO-LUMO gaps), then the whole model is fine-tuned on MS/MS spectra.
sections.source_locator: arXiv 2111.04824v3: Section 2.1, Figure 1, Section 4.4

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is the original implementation that accompanies the arXiv preprint (three versions; v3 dated 1 May 2023) and the Nature Machine Intelligence paper. The models in the manuscript were trained on the NIST 2020 MS/MS library, and NIST does not allow their parameters to be redistributed, so no manuscript checkpoints are released. The one public checkpoint is a demo model trained on MoNA with an InChIKey split (checkpoints/demo.pkl, from Zenodo record 8399738). Configs are provided to retrain on NIST and MoNA, including models at 1.0 Da and 0.1 Da bin sizes. A result should state the config file, the training data and whether NIST was used.

profile.summary: 3DMolMS (called MolMS in the FlexMS benchmark) predicts the tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of a compound from its 3D conformation. It takes a molecule with its precursor type and collision energy, generates a 3D conformation, encodes the atoms as a point set, and outputs a binned spectrum. The learned molecular representation can also be fine-tuned for retention time and collision cross section prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction; Bioinformatics paper abstract and Sections 2.1-2.3; FlexMS Section 3.2

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A 3D conformation is generated with the ETKDG algorithm in RDKit. Each atom becomes a point with its x, y, z coordinates and RDKit atom attributes, and bonds are represented by neighbouring vectors. In the paper, an encoder of six 3D molecular convolution layers (64 to 1024 dimensions) produces representations that are concatenated with metadata into a 2048-dimensional vector, and a decoder of five fully connected layers with residual blocks outputs the spectrum. By default spectra are binned at 0.2 resolution over m/z 0 to 1500, giving 7500 bins. Release v1.4.0 changed the encoder to aggregate over the covalent bond graph and replaced the decoder with a bidirectional head, so the current checkpoints are not the paper's architecture.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2.2-2.3; README.md: Latest release

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The package molnetpack has had many releases since v1.0.0 (2023-06-30). Notable changes: training data enlarged with MoNA and Waters QTOF data (v1.1.0), an Orbitrap MS/MS model (v1.1.6), an E(3)-invariant encoder (v1.3.1) and the bond-graph encoder with a bidirectional head (v1.4.0, 2026-08-11), for which all four checkpoints (QTOF, Orbitrap, RT, CCS) were retrained from geometric pretraining on ChEMBL. Release v1.4.0 has five zip assets, including a pretraining checkpoint. v1.4.0 checkpoints embed their training config and loading refuses mismatches; older checkpoints only give a warning. A result should name the package version and the checkpoint (qtof or orbitrap).

profile.summary: NEIMS (Neural Electron-Ionization Mass Spectrometry) predicts the electron ionization (EI) mass spectrum of a small molecule. It takes a molecule, turns it into a count-based circular fingerprint, and outputs a spectrum with an intensity for every integer m/z bin. The aim is to add predicted spectra to a reference library so that molecules missing from the library can still be matched.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods; README.md: Introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Molecules are mapped to additive (count) ECFP fingerprints of length 4096 and radius 2, computed with RDKit, and passed to a multilayer perceptron. The tuned MLP has seven layers of 2000 nodes with residual connections, ReLU and dropout 0.25. The output is adjusted for physical effects of ionisation: besides a forward prediction, a reverse prediction mode is added, because the authors found forward prediction struggles with large fragments from neutral losses, and the two are combined (bidirectional prediction). The model is written in TensorFlow.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods (Spectral Prediction, Adjustments for Physical Phenomena), Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one published model and one set of pretrained weights, linked from the README. When Rewire requested that weights URL anonymously on 2026-11-27, Google Cloud Storage returned an Access denied error, so the pretrained weights could not be confirmed as available. The repository is archived on GitHub. The train, validation and test molecules are provided in training_splits (InChIKey and SMILES). The paper's models were trained on 240 942 spectra from the NIST 2017 main library, which is not distributed with the code, so retraining the published model needs a NIST licence. A result should state whether it used the released weights or a retrained model, and on what data.

profile.summary: PerturbPFN predicts how cells respond to chemical perturbations whose targets are unknown. Given observed responses to other perturbations as context, it infers a latent gene graph, sparse intervention targets and intervention strengths, and propagates them through a causal (SCM) decoder to predict expression under a new perturbation. It is trained only on simulated perturbation episodes and has no released code or weights.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: PerturbPFN follows the prior-data fitted network (PFN) approach: a transformer is pre-trained on synthetic tasks so that at test time it predicts in context, without gradient updates. Each synthetic episode samples a modular, scale-free gene regulatory network, drug-like perturbations with sparse targets and Hill-type dose-response strengths, and zero-inflated log-normal observations with SERGIO noise. The model infers context interventions and an episode-level graph, predicts the query's targets and strengths with dedicated heads, and generates expression through a modulated SCM decoder in topological order. Training uses multi-task losses on the synthetic graph, target, strength and outcome labels.
sections.source_locator: arXiv Sections 2.3 and 2.4; Fig. 1

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper reports one selected checkpoint, taken at step 3100 of a 3500-step run, with 14.98M parameters, used for all reported results. No code or weights were found: on 2026-11-27 a GitHub repository search for perturbpfn returned a total count of 0 and Hugging Face model searches for perturbpfn and perturb-pfn returned empty lists. The paper's results cannot be reproduced from public artefacts.
sections.source_locator: arXiv Appendix B; GitHub and Hugging Face search responses

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Research on perturbation effect prediction for unseen drugs, target identification and regulatory structure discovery. The authors evaluate it on real single-cell chemical perturbation data (Srivatsan et al. 2020, massively multiplex chemical transcriptomics) and on synthetic benchmarks.

profile.summary: BERTax reads a DNA sequence and says which part of the tree of life it came from, without comparing it to a database of known genomes. It is a BERT model: the sequence is cut into overlapping three letter tokens and a transformer encoder reads them, and classification layers on top predict superkingdom, phylum and, in the released version, genus. The point of the method is novel organisms: when no close relative exists in a reference database, similarity search degrades, while BERTax works from the statistics of the sequence itself.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Significance, Introduction, Materials and Methods; README.md: Usage, Training BERTax models

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Training has two steps. First a BERT encoder is pretrained without labels on genomic fragments of a fixed length of 1,500 nucleotides, each cut into 500 three letter tokens and presented as two sentences of 250 tokens. Then the model is fine-tuned for classification: the [CLS] token output goes to three taxonomy layers in what the authors call the all-in-one architecture, where each rank's prediction also sees the higher ranks. The authors compared flat, nested and all-in-one arrangements and found all-in-one best. Fine-tuning ran for at most 16 epochs with early stopping, and class weights per rank to stop the model favouring frequent classes. At prediction time each rank also has an unknown class, used when a sequence looks unlike any trained class.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, Pretraining and Architectures, Results; README.md: Usage note on unknown

sections.title: What it can classify
sections.body: Four superkingdoms (archaea, bacteria, eukaryota and viruses), and a fixed list of phyla and genera that the README prints without giving counts. Anything outside those lists is likely to come back as unknown, and the authors say so plainly. The README also carries their recommendation to use BERTax for superkingdom and phylum, with genus possible but weaker, and points at the separate training repository for building a model that covers other taxa.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Compatible phyla and genera, Training BERTax models; Paper: Introduction

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published tool is one model: the downloadable version, built on the all-in-one architecture, trained on what the paper calls the final model dataset, and the only version that predicts genus as well. The weights are a single file, big_trainingset_all_fix_classes_selection.h5, distributed through the repository's latest release, and the tool is also packaged as a conda package and a Docker image. The paper additionally describes models trained on a closely related and a distantly related dataset, used for its comparisons; those are not the released tool. A result should name the model file, the sequence splitting mode and the window settings, since long sequences are chunked and the chunk predictions are averaged by default.

profile.summary: DeepMicrobes assigns short metagenomic sequencing reads to a species or a genus. It reads a sequence as a bag of 12-mers, embeds them, passes them through a bidirectional LSTM with self-attention, and outputs a label with a confidence score; read level labels are then turned into an abundance profile. Its motivation is metagenome assembled genomes: species found by assembly have no curated place in a taxonomic tree, which standard classifiers need, and DeepMicrobes is trained directly on such genome collections instead.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction, Materials and Methods; document/prediction.md; README.md

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A read is tokenised into k-mers, with 12 as the length used unless stated otherwise, and complementary k-mers share one embedding vector, which is why the vocabulary files are described as merged. The embedded tokens go through a bidirectional LSTM and a multi-head self-attention layer, which the authors found to be the best of seven architectures they built; the others, kept in the repository, are a ResNet-like CNN, a CNN plus LSTM hybrid, Seq2species, and embed plus pool, CNN or LSTM variants. Reads are classified in pairs: the tutorial takes interleaved paired-end reads and the authors recommend paired-end mode as more accurate than single-end. The output per pair is a label and a confidence score, and a separate step turns those into a species or genus profile.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, Materials and Methods; document/prediction.md; document/tfrecord.md: Prediction; DeepMicrobes-data README: Vocabulary

sections.title: Training data and compute
sections.body: The species model was trained on reads simulated from 2505 representative genomes of human gut species, most of them identified by metagenome assembly, together with the taxonomy above species level. Reads were simulated with ART using a HiSeq 2500 error model, paired-end with an insert size of 400 and a standard deviation of 50 bp, then trimmed from the 3 prime end to between 75 and 150 bp with equal probability, and each read labelled by its species or genus. A pair was treated as two single-end reads during training. Training used TensorFlow on an NVIDIA Tesla P40 24GB GPU, with 30 randomly sampled hyperparameter settings per architecture and the best chosen on an evaluation set.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Materials and Methods, training set construction, implementation

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two things vary and must be named in any result: the taxonomic level, because the species and genus models are separate weight sets and the level flag has to match the weights, and the architecture, because the repository ships seven of them behind a --model_name option. The README also states that a new beta version is available, without a version number. No tag or release listing was saved, so whether a release carries the weights was not checked. The vocabulary file must match the k-mer length used, and the 12-mer vocabulary is the one the pretrained models use.

profile.summary: Stack is a single-cell foundation model that reads a set of cells from one sample together, so each cell's representation is informed by the other cells in its context. It takes cell-by-gene count matrices and outputs cell embeddings; through in-context learning it can also generate expression profiles for a target cell population under a condition shown by unlabelled prompt cells, such as a drug or a different donor.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stack is an encoder-decoder with tabular attention: layers alternate between attention across cells and attention across genes. Genes are compressed into a small number of trainable gene-group tokens (100 by default), and the input is a cell set drawn from a single experimental sample. Pre-training uses a rectangular mask: a random list of genes is masked for all cells in a mini-batch, with a mask ratio sampled between 0.1 and 0.8, and the model reconstructs each cell's expression distribution. A post-training stage uses a frozen teacher (self-distillation) so the student learns to predict target cell distributions conditioned on prompt cells.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Methods; README.md: Model Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two checkpoints are on Hugging Face. Stack-Large (bc_large.ckpt) is pre-trained on human scBaseCount for 10 epochs and has 217M parameters according to its card; the card points to the embedding tutorial. Stack-Large-Aligned (bc_large_aligned.ckpt) adds alignment on CellxGene 45M and Parse 10M PBMC for 8 epochs and points to the prediction tutorial. The paper reports configurations from 69 to 629 million parameters. A result should name the checkpoint file and Hugging Face revision.
sections.source_locator: Model cards; Hugging Face API responses; paper Results

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Embedding single-cell data, zero-shot prediction of unseen perturbation or observation profiles by in-context generation, and fine-tuning with a frozen teacher.

profile.summary: Tahoe-x1 (Tx1) is a family of single-cell foundation models, up to 3 billion parameters, pretrained on single-cell transcriptomes including the Tahoe-100M drug perturbation compendium. It takes single-cell expression data (genes by Ensembl ID) and outputs cell and gene embeddings, learned jointly with compound representations, for tasks such as gene essentiality, cell-type classification and perturbation response prediction.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Tx1 is a transformer encoder pretrained with a masked-expression objective; the authors credit scGPT as inspiration for the architecture. Each gene token combines a gene embedding with a continuous expression encoding, and a CLS token gives the cell embedding. In the 3B configuration only, a chemical encoder adds a drug token (fp_dim: 2048, num_drugs: 378); the 1B and 70M configs have no chemical encoder block. The 3B configuration has 32 layers, model width 2560 and 20 heads; the 1B has 24 layers, width 2048, 16 heads; the 70M has 12 layers, width 512, 8 heads. Training uses FlashAttention on the MosaicML Composer and llm-foundry stack.

sections.body: Three checkpoints are released in one Hugging Face repository, in folders 70m-model, 1b-model and 3b-model, and on S3. The README calls them Tx1-70M (70M, context 1024), Tx1-1.3B (1.3B, context 2048) and Tx1-3B (3B, context 2048); the model card calls the middle one Tx1-1B with about 1.3B parameters. The README notes that the current code supports only FlashAttention without custom attention masks, while Tx1-1B and Tx1-70M were trained with the Triton backend and custom masks. A result should name the checkpoint folder, the Hugging Face revision and the repository commit.

profile.summary: FlowDock predicts the three dimensional structure of a protein-ligand complex and, at the same time, how strongly the ligand binds. The inputs are protein sequences and ligand SMILES strings, with no pocket and no multiple sequence alignment needed; the model first predicts an unbound protein structure with ESMFold, then moves it towards a bound structure. Each generated complex comes with a structural confidence score and a binding affinity value, and several ligands can be modelled at the same time.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Section 3 overview; README.md: Description, How to predict new protein-ligand complex structures and their affinities

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FlowDock is a conditional flow matching model: it learns a path from an unbound (apo) protein structure to the bound (holo) structure, for any number of binding ligands. The protein side starts from an ESMFold structure, which the authors use as a surrogate prior, and the ligand side starts from a harmonic prior constrained by the bond graph of the given SMILES string. The network is the NeuralPLexer architecture, which encodes protein language model sequence embeddings and ligand SMILES strings and decodes contact maps that condition a flow ordinary differential equation for the coordinates. The authors fine-tune NeuralPLexer's score head with the flow matching objective, along with its other intermediate weights and heads, including a confidence head redesigned to predict binding affinity; NeuralPLexer's original confidence head stays frozen.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Section 3 Methods, structure parametrisation and optimisation

sections.title: Training data and compute
sections.body: Training used PDBBind-E, which the authors describe as an enhanced version of a PDBBind 2020 based training set: they collected 17 743 crystal complex structures from PDBBind 2020 and 47 183 structures from the Binding MOAD. The repository also ships preparation steps for DockGen and a PDB based van der Mers dataset, and a fine-tuning route on PLINDER, which it warns needs about an hour to download and about 750G of storage. The paper states that FlowDock was trained using only 4 80GB H100 GPUs for 1 week, which it contrasts with the 128 A100 GPUs for one month it attributes to Chai-1.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 3 dataset curation, Section 4 results discussion; README.md: How to prepare data for FlowDock

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published weights are a tar archive on Zenodo record 15066450, and the commands in the README name two checkpoints from it: esmfold_prior_paper_weights.ckpt for fine-tuning and esmfold_prior_paper_weights-EMA.ckpt for evaluation and sampling. The pretrained NeuralPLexer weights are a separate download, from Zenodo record 10373581. A result should name the checkpoint, the prior type, the sampler and the number of steps, since those are all command line settings; the README's examples use prior_type=esmfold, sampler=VDODE, num_steps=40 and n_samples=5. The repository also ships a Dockerfile and points at a prebuilt image.

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: The NeuralPLexer architecture, fine-tuned with a flow matching objective: protein language model sequence embeddings and ligand SMILES are encoded, block diagonal contact maps are decoded to condition a flow ODE on the coordinates, and separate confidence and affinity heads score each sample.

profile.summary: FLOWR.root designs ligands inside a protein pocket and scores how strongly they would bind, with one model. Given a protein structure and a reference ligand that marks the pocket, it generates three dimensional ligands, and its affinity head predicts four endpoints (pIC50, pKi, pKd, pEC50) with a confidence estimate for the generated structure. The same model can instead score ligands you already have, and it can be adapted to a project's own compounds with low rank fine-tuning.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results overview; README.md: Predicting Binding Affinities, Generating Molecules from PDB/CIF; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The model is an SE(3)-equivariant flow matching framework: it learns to transport an initial ligand sample towards a plausible bound ligand in a given pocket, and the structure head, the affinity head and a pLDDT style confidence head share one backbone. Because structure and affinity are trained together, the affinity prediction can steer generation at inference time by importance sampling instead of calling an external scoring function. The architecture uses a pocket encoder and a ligand decoder with latent attention, 128 coordinate sets, a latent size of 64 and 32 attention heads. The paper gives about 33 million trainable parameters for its configuration, whose ligand decoder has width 384; the README puts the released joint affinity checkpoints at d_model 512, so the count is not tied to a released checkpoint. Training ran in three stages: pretraining on about 1.5B small molecule conformations and about 2.5M mixed fidelity protein-ligand complexes, refinement on the curated SPINDR and HiQBind co-crystal sets, then project specific adaptation with LoRA.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results overview, Methods architecture and training

sections.title: What it can be asked to do
sections.body: From a protein PDB or CIF file plus a reference ligand, the repository supports de novo pocket conditional generation, interaction and pharmacophore conditional sampling, scaffold hopping and elaboration, core growing, fragment growing, and local replacement of chosen atoms by substructure inpainting. A separate ligand only mode generates without a protein context, using its own checkpoint. Affinity prediction is a different entry point: it scores the ligand you give it and writes the scores back into an SDF file, and a multi ligand variant scores many ligands against one protein in a single job, averaging over several seeds.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Generating Molecules from PDB/CIF, Generating Molecules from SDF, Predicting Binding Affinities; Paper: Abstract; predict_aff.sl

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Four checkpoints are published on Google Drive, and the paper says pretrained checkpoints are mirrored on Zenodo. flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt is the latest joint generation and affinity model, flowr_root_v2.ckpt is the model behind most results in the paper and is the one the authors name for reproduction, flowr_root_spindr_base.ckpt is a fully converged generation only model trained on SPINDR, and flowr_root_v2_mol.ckpt is the ligand only model. They differ in architecture flags, which must be passed by hand when warm starting: d_model 512 with no cross products and an affinity head for v2.2 and v2.1, d_model 384 with cross products and no affinity head for spindr and v2_mol. A result must therefore name the checkpoint, the flags and the seed; the README warns that a fixed seed gives different samples on CPU, MPS and CUDA.

strengths.text: Generation and affinity scoring come from one model, so predicted affinity can steer sampling at inference time without an external scoring function.

Four affinity endpoints are predicted separately, pIC50, pKi, pKd and pEC50, rather than mixed into one score. The paper describes this as explicitly avoiding treating heterogeneous affinity labels as interchangeable.
The paper describes a small model, about 33 million trainable parameters for the configuration it reports, and the LoRA route adapts it with about 3.3M trainable parameters.
strengths.source_locator: Paper: Methods architecture, Methods LoRA finetuning

strengths.text: The release is unusually complete: MIT code with a locked dependency set, four checkpoints, datasets, SLURM scripts for generation, prediction, training and both fine-tuning routes, and a browser interface.

limitations.text: The authors say the joint affinity and generation model is not fully converged, because of computational constraints, and that clash count can be a problem on out of distribution data.
The affinity head is described as accurate in distribution only. For out of distribution data, such as in-series compounds, the authors say it should be combined with LoRA adaptation.

It needs a large GPU in practice: the README recommends a CUDA GPU with at least 40GB VRAM for inference, and says CPU inference takes minutes rather than seconds. Apple MPS is opt-in and unvalidated.

The checkpoints differ in architecture flags that are not read back from the file, so a warm start with the shipped training script fails unless the flags are changed by hand; the README states its shipped flags do not match flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt.

run_guide.summary: Install the environment with uv, fetch a checkpoint, and score a ligand against a protein pocket to get predicted affinities.
prerequisites: uv as the package manager. The README says FLOWR.root requires Python 3.12 and that uv fetches a matching interpreter from the pin in pyproject.toml.
A CUDA GPU with at least 40GB VRAM is recommended for inference; CPU and macOS installs work through the cpu extra, with inference taking minutes rather than seconds.
A checkpoint from the Google Drive folder the README links, for example flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt for joint generation and affinity.
A prepared protein PDB or CIF file and a ligand file, protonated, as the README recommends.
On macOS, run with --num_workers 0; the README explains that higher values fail there.

steps.title: Predict affinities for one protein and ligand
steps.shell:
uv run --no-sync python -m flowr.predict.predict_from_pdb \
    --pdb_file YOUR_PROTEIN.pdb \
    --ligand_file YOUR_LIGAND.sdf \
    --dataset YOUR_PROTEIN_NAME \
    --gpus 1 \
    --num_workers 12 \
    --seed 42 \
    --batch_cost 20 \
    --arch pocket \
    --pocket_type holo \
    --pocket_noise fix \
    --cut_pocket \
    --pocket_cutoff 7 \
    --ckpt_path /path/to/flowr_root_v2.2.ckpt \
    --save_dir ./predict-aff_seed-42

profile.summary: Graph_RG is a protein-ligand binding affinity predictor that does not need a docked pose or a complex structure. It was the author's entry in the small molecule affinity prediction category of CASP16, the 2024 community prediction experiment. Because it does not search over conformations, the author reports it as fast enough for very large virtual screens. The sources read name no code or weights and the paper is not open access, so what the model reads as input and how it is built are not described here.

The abstract says only that the method is pose-free and not dependent on the protein-ligand complex, which is what the author credits for its speed, and that possible improvements include dataset optimisation, atomic vector representation and model architecture upgrades. The paper itself is not open access and no repository is named in the sources read, so the layers, the training objective and the input features are not established here. profile.summary: GraphDTA predicts how strongly a drug molecule binds a target protein. The drug is given as a molecular graph rather than a string, and the protein as its amino acid sequence; the output is a single affinity value. The point of the method is the drug side: the authors argue that a graph is a more natural representation of a molecule than a SMILES string, and they encode it with a graph neural network while a one dimensional convolution reads the protein sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: Europe PMC record: abstractText, Summary; models/ginconv.py: GINConvNet

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The drug is turned into a graph of atoms with 78 features per node, and one of four graph networks encodes it: GINConvNet, GATNet, GAT_GCN or GCNNet. In GINConvNet, five GIN convolution layers of width 32 with batch normalisation are followed by sum pooling and a linear layer to a 128 wide drug vector. The protein sequence is mapped character by character to integers, cut or padded to 1000 positions, embedded with width 128, and passed through a single one dimensional convolution with 32 filters and a kernel of 8, then a linear layer to a 128 wide protein vector. The two vectors are concatenated and sent through dense layers of 1024 and 256 units to one output unit, trained with mean squared error.
sections.source_locator: models/ginconv.py: GINConvNet; create_data.py: seq_cat, max_seq_len; training.py: loss_fn; README.md: Source codes

sections.title: Data and training settings
sections.body: The repository ships the Davis and KIBA datasets, which the README says were downloaded from the DeepDTA repository, with the fold files that define the split. For Davis the preparation script converts the affinities to a log scale. Training runs for 1000 epochs with a batch size of 512 and Adam at a learning rate of 0.0005. Two scripts differ in how the best model is chosen: training.py keeps the model with the best mean squared error on the test data, following DeepDTA's practice, while training_validation.py holds out 20 per cent of the training data and selects on that instead.

sections.body: The four drug encoders are the versions that matter: a result must say which of GINConvNet, GATNet, GAT_GCN and GCNNet was used, on which dataset, and with which of the two training scripts, because the selection rule differs between them. The code was read here at commit 6162245c6776684b391d30610850fe7077478435. The paper's availability statement says pre-trained models are at the repository; the file listing at this commit contains no model file, and the sources read do not explain the difference. profile.summary: MolForge is a set of transformer models that translate a molecular fingerprint back into a molecule, written as SMILES or SELFIES. The input is the list of set bits of a structural fingerprint (for example ECFP4) and the output is a decoded molecular string. In mass spectrometry work it is used as the second stage of de novo structure generation: a spectrum encoder such as MIST predicts a fingerprint, and MolForge decodes it into candidate structures.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and Prediction & Demo; paper Model overview; Neo et al. abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MolForge treats fingerprint-to-molecule conversion as translation. The fingerprint's set bits are tokens on the source side and SMILES or SELFIES tokens on the target side, each with its own vocabulary file (ECFP4_vocab_sp and smiles_vocab_sp in the README demo). A later paper that reuses MolForge describes its SMILES tokenizer as SentencePiece. The model is a standard encoder-decoder Transformer: six encoder and six decoder layers with eight attention heads, 512-dimensional attention and 2048-dimensional feed-forward layers, with layer normalisation before each sub-layer. Each fingerprint and output representation pair is a separate model, trained with a negative log-likelihood loss on two GPUs for up to 500 K steps. Decoding is greedy or beam search.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Model overview, Training; README.md: Prediction & Demo

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The authors trained one model per fingerprint and output representation; the README's results table covers 15 fingerprint encodings including MACCS, Avalon, RDK4, atom pairs, topological torsions, ECFP0 to ECFP4, FCFP2, FCFP4 and atomic environments. Checkpoints are shared as two Google Drive archives: the top-performing models and all other models. The demo loads saved_models/ECFP4_smiles_checkpoint.pth. A result should name the fingerprint, the output representation (smiles or selfies), the checkpoint and the decoding method.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Prediction & Demo, Result

sections.title: Use with mass spectra and in benchmarks
sections.body: Neo et al. (2025) paired a MIST spectrum encoder with a MolForge decoder, thresholded fingerprint bit probabilities, and reported top-1 31% and top-10 40% on MassSpecGym. The MassSpecGym in the Wild paper (an existing source on this record) retrained MolForge decoders on 2.5M, 10M and 50M molecule corpora with the public MolForge code and a 4096-bit Morgan fingerprint preset, paired with a freshly trained MIST encoder. It reports that the earlier MIST + MolForge results were inflated by a batched-inference problem with a reused MIST checkpoint: top-1 accuracy was 31.75% with batch size 24 and 10.73% after correction, and it marks the inflated figures as not valid.
sections.source_locator: Neo et al. abstract; MassSpecGym in the Wild: Appendix (MolForge Training and Inference Configuration), Section 6.1.2, Table 4

profile.summary: SCimilarity is a model for searching large single-cell RNA-seq atlases for cells similar to a query cell. It takes a cell's normalised expression profile and outputs a 128-dimensional embedding in which similar cell states lie close together, so a query can be matched against a reference of 23.4 million cells, and cells can be annotated, without retraining on new studies.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.rst; paper Fig. 1 legend and Methods

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A fully connected encoder reduces 28,231 genes through hidden layers of 1,024, 1,024, 1,024 and 128 units; the 128-dimensional output is scaled to unit length, so embeddings lie on a hypersphere. Training combines a triplet loss, which uses Cell Ontology annotations to pull cells of the same type together and push different types apart, with a mean squared error reconstruction loss from a decoder that preserves finer variation. Training uses heavy dropout (40% on the input, 50% on hidden layers).

sections.body: The pretrained model is distributed on Zenodo as model_v1.1.tar.gz (record version 1.1), which bundles model weights, embeddings, kNN graphs and metadata; Zenodo says it is meant for SCimilarity API v0.2.0. The tutorial's text links a different Zenodo record (8240464) while its download command uses record 10685499. A result should name model v1.1 and the API version.

profile.summary: FLARE (Fine-grained Learning for Alignment of spectra-molecule REpresentations) annotates metabolites from tandem mass spectra by retrieval. It embeds an MS/MS spectrum, written as chemical formulas for each peak, and candidate molecular graphs in a shared space, then ranks the candidates by similarity. The similarity is built from peak-to-atom and atom-to-peak matches, so the matches can be inspected.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Peaks are first given chemical formulas by a MIST-style subformula assigner. Each formula peak is projected by a shallow MLP and contextualised by a transformer encoder, giving one embedding per peak. The molecule is a graph whose nodes carry atom features, encoded by a graph convolutional network into node embeddings. Training uses a fine-grained contrastive loss (filipContrastive): the similarity of a spectrum and a molecule averages the maximum peak-to-node and node-to-peak cosine similarities, with a temperature-scaled loss. At test time candidates are ranked by this similarity.
sections.source_locator: Paper Methods; Space README: Overview, Model (default stack)

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Code and the released checkpoint (pretrained_models/flare.ckpt) are distributed in the Hugging Face Space HassounLab/FLARE, which the paper names as the code location; no separate GitHub repository is named. Paper recipes are in run_scripts: the main FLARE model with candidates by mass or by formula, a global pooling baseline, and an evaluation with msbuddy-predicted formulas. The evaluation scripts use the released checkpoint by default. The Space was last modified on 2026-10-22. profile.summary: JESTR (Joint Embedding Space Technique for Ranking) annotates metabolites from tandem mass spectra. It embeds a query MS/MS spectrum and each candidate molecule into one shared space and ranks the candidates by cosine similarity, without predicting a fingerprint or simulating a spectrum. The candidates are typically molecules from PubChem with the right mass or formula.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The molecule encoder is a graph convolutional network over atom and bond features, followed by max pooling and two fully connected layers. The spectrum is binned into 1 Da bins up to 1000 Da (peaks above are dropped), intensities are normalised and log-transformed, and the 1000-dimension vector is passed through a three-layer MLP. The two encoders are trained with a contrastive InfoNCE loss so that a spectrum and its molecule are close. Late in training the model is regularised with candidate molecules that share a formula with training molecules, which the authors report improves rank@1.
sections.source_locator: Paper Section 2.1 Encoders; abstract; Methods on regularisation

The NPLIB1 data is included, with large files on Zenodo; NIST and other licensed datasets used in the paper are not released. The released weights are for GPU-trained models. A result should name the weight set (NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym) and whether candidate regularisation was used.

profile.summary: MVP (MultiView Projection) ranks candidate molecules for a tandem mass spectrum to annotate metabolites. It learns one embedding space for four views of the same compound: the molecular graph, the molecular fingerprint, a single spectrum and a consensus spectrum built from several spectra of that compound. A query spectrum or consensus spectrum is then compared with candidate molecules in that space.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MVP has one encoder per view and a contrastive loss over every pair of views. The molecule encoder is the same as JESTR's: a 3-layer graph convolutional network, a pooling layer and two fully connected layers. Spectra and consensus spectra are sets of peaks; by default each peak is represented by its chemical formula (FormSpec), encoded by a 3-layer MLP and then a transformer encoder with 2 attention heads. A binned-spectrum variant (BinnedSpec) is also provided. At inference any molecule view can be paired with any spectrum view; the authors report the graph to consensus spectrum view (mol-cs) as best.

profile.summary: TranscriptFormer is a family of generative single-cell foundation models trained on up to 112 million cells from 12 species. It reads a cell's raw counts (genes by Ensembl ID) and models gene identities and expression levels jointly; its cell embeddings are used for cross-species cell type classification, disease state identification and transfer of annotations, and the generative model can be prompted for cell type-specific transcription factors and gene-gene interactions.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: TranscriptFormer is a generative autoregressive joint model over genes and their expression levels in a cell, built on a transformer with coupled gene and transcript heads, expression-aware multi-head self-attention, causal masking and a count likelihood. The README says the non-trainable parameters come from frozen pretrained embeddings, that each model comes with protein embeddings for its training species, and that protein embeddings for new species can be generated with ESM-2. Cell embeddings are mean-pooled over the genes of a cell; contextual gene embeddings are the per-gene transformer outputs.

profile.summary: DiffMS generates candidate molecular structures from a tandem mass spectrum (de novo structure elucidation). It takes an MS/MS spectrum and the molecule's chemical formula, encodes the spectrum with a formula transformer, and uses a discrete graph diffusion model to build molecular graphs with the right heavy atoms. It outputs a set of sampled candidate structures.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The encoder is the MIST formula transformer, which embeds spectrum peaks labelled with formulas and neutral losses. The decoder is a discrete graph diffusion model adapted from DiGress: it denoises an adjacency matrix over a fixed set of heavy atoms taken from the known formula, and hydrogens are placed implicitly. The decoder is pretrained on 2.8M fingerprint-molecule pairs (2048-bit Morgan fingerprints, radius 2) from DSSTox, HMDB, COCONUT and MOSES; the encoder is pretrained on the finetuning data (NPLIB1 or MassSpecGym); then the whole model is finetuned with the denoising cross-entropy loss.

profile.summary: FRIGID generates candidate molecular structures from a tandem mass spectrum (de novo structure elucidation). A MIST encoder predicts a molecular fingerprint from the spectrum, and a masked diffusion language model generates molecules as SAFE strings conditioned on that fingerprint and the chemical formula. An optional refinement loop simulates spectra of the candidates with the ICEBERG forward model and re-generates the parts that do not match.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stage 1 (FRIGID-base): a MIST encoder predicts a 4096-bit radius-2 Morgan fingerprint; its active bits are embedded and passed through 3 self-attention layers, and the precursor formula is encoded as per-element counts; both enter every Transformer block through cross-attention. The backbone is a 12-layer BERT-style masked diffusion language model (hidden size 896, 14 heads) over BPE-tokenised SAFE strings, and an NGBoost model predicts the sequence length from the formula. Stage 2: candidates are ranked against the predicted fingerprint, ICEBERG simulates their spectra, peaks that appear in simulation but not in the experiment flag inconsistent atoms, and those tokens are re-masked and re-denoised over several rounds. The code is adapted from NVIDIA's GenMol.
sections.source_locator: README.md: How It Works, Model Architecture Details

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README reports that earlier MIST encoders for MassSpecGym were trained with synthetic spectra of PubChem molecules chosen to resemble test formulas, which used test-set information. The encoders were replaced (MIST 2M-aug for NPLIB1, MIST 4M-aug for MassSpecGym), the evaluations repeated, and the earlier results marked as superseded: for example FRIGID on MassSpecGym fell from 18.29% to 9.05% top-1 accuracy. The updated release (Zenodo record 23543494, 2026-10-21, Apache 2.0) holds DLM.ckpt and four ICEBERG checkpoints; MIST encoders come from a separate Zenodo record. The paper read is arXiv v3 (25 Oct 2026). A result should state which MIST encoder was used, whether refinement was applied and how many rounds.

profile.summary: ChemBERTa is a family of transformer language models trained on SMILES strings, the text notation for molecules. Given a SMILES string, a model returns embeddings that can be fine-tuned or used as features for molecular property prediction. ChemBERTa-2, the version cited by the benchmark source, is pretrained on up to 77M PubChem compounds with either masked language modelling or multi-task regression.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ChemBERTa-2 uses the RoBERTa transformer implementation in Hugging Face. Masked language modelling (MLM) masks 15% of SMILES tokens and trains the model to recover them; multi-task regression (MTR) trains it to predict 200 molecular properties computed with RDKit from the SMILES. The vocabulary is at most 591 tokens and sequences at most 512 tokens. The authors searched 50 configurations of 5M to 46M parameters on a 5M-compound set, then trained selected ones on 10M and 77M compounds. They report that MTR pretraining gives better downstream results but trains more slowly.
sections.source_locator: ChemBERTa-2 Methods and Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The paper compares MLM and MTR models pretrained on 5M, 10M and 77M compounds, alongside the original ChemBERTa, and says the trained models are open-sourced. The DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MLM checkpoint on Hugging Face is a 3-layer RoBERTa masked language model (hidden size 384, 12 heads, vocabulary 600) with no model card. MassSpecGym in the Wild also used a checkpoint published under a different Hugging Face account, Derify/ChemBERTa_augmented_pubchem_13m (43,963,205 parameters, Apache-2.0, trained on an augmented 13M PubChem set). A result should name the exact Hugging Face repository and revision.

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) did not evaluate ChemBERTa as a spectrum model. It used ChemBERTa encoders to show a shortcut in the MassSpecGym retrieval candidates: a frozen ChemBERTa-2 encoder (Derify/ChemBERTa_augmented_pubchem_13m) aligned with DreaMS spectrum embeddings, and a spectrum-blind classifier fine-tuned from DeepChem/ChemBERTa-77M-MLM. Because true molecules kept non-canonical SMILES while decoys were RDKit-canonicalised, these models could rank the true molecule first from formatting alone; MassSpecGym v1.5 canonicalises all SMILES by default.

profile.summary: Chemformer is a BART-style transformer language model for chemistry that reads and writes SMILES strings. It is pretrained to reconstruct original SMILES from corrupted or randomised ones, and then fine-tuned for sequence-to-sequence tasks such as reaction and retrosynthesis prediction or for property prediction. Inputs are SMILES strings; outputs are predicted SMILES or property values.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md introduction; paper abstract and Section 2

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each molecule is written as a non-canonical SMILES string, randomly modified, tokenised and embedded with sinusoidal positions. A bidirectional encoder reads the modified string and an autoregressive decoder is trained with cross-entropy to output the original SMILES. After pretraining, the weights are fine-tuned for each task. Chemformer (base) uses the original Transformer sizes: model dimension 512, feed-forward 2048, 6 layers, 8 heads, about 45M parameters. Chemformer-Large has about 230M.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2 and 2.1-2.4, Table 1

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds the code for three Chemformer papers and has been replaced by AiZynthModels, which includes an updated Chemformer. Public pretrained models and datasets are on a Box share; checkpoints from older versions need a key renamed (vocab_size to vocabulary_size) before use with the current code. The paper pretrained base and Large models on about 100 million ZINC-15 SMILES. A result should name the checkpoint file and the code version.
sections.source_locator: README.md introduction; paper Section 2.1

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source
sections.body: MassSpecGym in the Wild (an existing source on this record) did not evaluate Chemformer as a spectrum model. It built a two-stage retrieval pipeline on a frozen ChemFormer BART encoder (d = 512, 6 layers, 8 heads, 523-token vocabulary) paired with a trained spectrum encoder, and showed that it reached over 63% hit rate@1 by exploiting a SMILES canonicalisation difference between true molecules and decoys in the MassSpecGym candidates.

profile.summary: scBERT is a pretrained deep language model for annotating cell types in single-cell RNA-seq data. It is first pre-trained on large amounts of unlabelled scRNA-seq data to learn gene-gene interactions, then fine-tuned on a labelled reference; the fine-tuned model takes a normalised expression profile and outputs the cell type of each cell, and can flag novel cell types by thresholding prediction confidence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: scBERT follows BERT's pre-train and fine-tune approach with a Performer encoder. Expression values are binned into a small number of tokens (num_tokens, default 7 in the README) and combined with a gene embedding; predict.py uses Gene2vec encoding for genes by default and a sequence of 16906 genes plus one. The default encoder has 6 layers, 10 heads and a 200-dimensional embedding. For annotation a classifier head is trained on top during fine-tuning.
