sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained checkpoint is offered through a Weixin Drive link, with no version label or checksum. Users fine-tune it on their own labelled data, so every annotation result depends on the fine-tuning data. predict.py sets bin_num to 5 by default and builds the model with num_tokens = bin_num + 2 = 7, which matches the README's default num_tokens of 7 (the README calls this the number of bins). A result should name the repository commit, the checkpoint source and the fine-tuning data.

profile.summary: FOAM (Formula-constrained Optimization for Annotating Metabolites) proposes molecular structures for an unknown tandem mass spectrum by optimisation rather than by a single trained generator. Given the spectrum and the molecular formula, it starts from seed structures with that formula, evolves them with a formula-constrained graph genetic algorithm, and keeps the candidates whose ICEBERG-simulated spectra best match the observed one. Seeds can come from PubChem or from other models such as DiffMS.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: FOAM first retrieves seed structures that match the formula (from PubChem, with the true structure excluded in evaluation, or from another tool). ICEBERG simulates the spectrum of each candidate, candidates are scored by similarity to the observed spectrum, and the best form a mating pool. A graph genetic algorithm then applies crossover and mutation that keep the formula fixed, and the loop repeats until a budget of ICEBERG calls is used. A multi-objective variant adds a penalty on structural complexity. FOAM has no trained weights of its own; the learned part is the ICEBERG simulator.
sections.source_locator: Paper Section 2 and Figure 1; README.md

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Reproduction configs are in configs/final, for NIST'20 (7,500 calls) and MassSpecGym with PubChem and DiffMS seeds. The MassSpecGym ICEBERG checkpoints (msg_gen.ckpt and msg_inten_cosine.ckpt) and the PubChem and DiffMS seed caches are on Zenodo record 18502041 (CC-BY-4.0, published 2026-02-06). The NIST'20 ICEBERG weights and NIST spectra are not public. A result should name the config, the seed sources, the call budget and the ICEBERG checkpoints.

It gives the MassSpecGym call budget as 5,000 in its results and 1,500 in its methods, and the repository's MassSpecGym config is named for 1,500 calls. The sources do not say which setting the leaderboard row used.

profile.summary: MADGEN (Mass-spec Attends to De Novo Molecular GENeration) generates molecular structures from a tandem mass spectrum in two stages. First it retrieves the molecule's core scaffold (its Murcko ring framework) by ranking candidate scaffolds against the spectrum; then a spectrum-guided generative model adds the remaining atoms and bonds, using the chemical formula to fix which atoms are present. It outputs sampled candidate molecules.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Stage 1 treats scaffold retrieval as ranking: contrastive learning aligns spectra (with their formula) with candidate Murcko scaffolds, and the top-ranked scaffold is chosen; an oracle retriever that is given the true scaffold is used to measure stage 2 alone. Stage 2 starts from the scaffold and the formula's atoms and generates the missing bonds with a Markov bridge process adapted from RetroBridge, using attention to bring spectral information into every step. The generator is a 5-layer graph transformer. The paper gives 50 diffusion steps in one passage and a 100-step Markov bridge in its training details; the README samples with --n_steps 100.
sections.source_locator: Paper abstract and Sections 3.1-3.2

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two pretrained generators are released on Zenodo record 17115068 (CC-BY-4.0): msgym.ckpt (MassSpecGym) and canopus.ckpt (CANOPUS), together with processed data, predicted scaffold rankings and scaffold-retrieval datasets. The NIST23 model and data are not public because NIST is licensed. The paper read is arXiv v4 (29 Apr 2025), published at ICLR 2025. A result should say whether the predictive or the oracle scaffold retriever was used, because the gap is large.

profile.summary: MS-BART generates molecular structures from tandem mass spectra by treating the task as translation between token sequences. A MIST encoder first turns the spectrum into a predicted molecular fingerprint; MS-BART reads the fingerprint bits as tokens and writes the molecule as a SELFIES string, using one vocabulary for both. It is pretrained on 4 million simulated fingerprint-molecule pairs, fine-tuned on experimental spectra and then aligned with chemical feedback.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The backbone is BART-base trained from scratch. Inputs are fingerprints predicted by MIST and binarised with a threshold (0.2 for NPLIB1, 0.11 for MassSpecGym); outputs are canonical SELFIES from a 185-token vocabulary. Pretraining combines three span-denoising tasks and one fingerprint-to-molecule translation task on 4M simulated pairs built from MassSpecGym's unlabelled molecules, excluding molecules close to the test fold. The model is then fine-tuned on MIST fingerprints of experimental spectra, and finally aligned with a chemical feedback step that favours molecules closer to the reference.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 3.1-3.4, Implementation, Appendix

sections.body: The original release on Figshare (article 30393544, CC BY 4.0, published 2025-10-19) holds, for CANOPUS and MassSpecGym, the final model weights, pretrained models, MIST checkpoints and preprocessed data. The current README also supports alternative MIST encoders from FRIGID for the fingerprint step, and notes known path and variable errors in its evaluation scripts. A result should state the MIST encoder, the fingerprint threshold and which stage (pretrained, fine-tuned or aligned) was evaluated.

profile.summary: MSNovelist generates candidate molecular structures de novo from a tandem mass spectrum. SIRIUS and CSI:FingerID first predict the molecular formula and a molecular fingerprint from the spectrum; an encoder-decoder recurrent neural network then writes SMILES strings that fit the fingerprint and formula, and candidates are ranked by how well they match the predicted fingerprint. The authors now point users to SIRIUS 6, where MSNovelist is integrated.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: MSNovelist splits the problem in two. CSI:FingerID maps the spectrum to a high-dimensional molecular fingerprint, and SIRIUS predicts the formula. Instead of searching a database with the fingerprint, an RNN generates structures: the fingerprint and formula are encoded into a starting state, and a three-layer LSTM decoder writes the SMILES character by character, in analogy to image captioning. Because the generator learns from structures rather than spectra, it was trained on 1,232,184 structures from HMDB, COCONUT and DSSTox, with simulated fingerprint errors added. Candidates are ranked by a modified Platt score against the predicted fingerprint.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published version depended on SIRIUS 4.4.29, whose backend no longer runs, so the Docker workflow in the README is marked obsolete. MSNovelist was integrated into SIRIUS 6 and retrained there on new SIRIUS 6 data; the repository is mostly that backend and cannot be used directly without retraining on other fingerprint data. A mist branch, merged into the repository, has early work on using predicted 4096-bit Morgan fingerprints. A result should say whether it used the published model, the SIRIUS 6 version, or a retrained model on another fingerprint (such as MIST + MSNovelist).

profile.summary: Neuraldecipher reverse-engineers extended-connectivity fingerprints (ECFPs) back to molecular structures. A feed-forward network maps an ECFP to a continuous molecular descriptor (CDDD), and the pretrained CDDD decoder of Winter et al. turns that descriptor into a SMILES string. It was built to test whether shared fingerprints can reveal confidential structures; in mass spectrometry work it has been used as a fingerprint-to-molecule decoder after a spectrum encoder.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Section 2; MassSpecGym in the Wild Table 9

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The Neuraldecipher is a standard feed-forward network with fully connected layers. Its input is an ECFP of length k (binary or count); its output is a point in the 512-dimensional CDDD space. It is trained to minimise the distance between predicted and true CDDD vectors (optionally with a cosine loss). The fixed CDDD decoder, an RNN with three stacked recurrent layers, then decodes the vector to SMILES; using it means the Neuraldecipher does not have to learn SMILES syntax itself.
sections.source_locator: Paper Sections 2 and 2.1; README.md: Training

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository ships one trained model: ECFP6 with 1024 bits, trained on the cluster split (models/1024_final_model_cs_gpu/weights.pt), evaluated in source/evaluation.ipynb. Parameter files for other ECFP settings are in params/. The CDDD decoder comes from a separate repository and must be installed in the same environment. A result should state the ECFP length, radius, binary or count form, and the split.

profile.summary: Spec2Mol recommends molecular structures from tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) alone. An encoder turns a set of four spectra of a compound (positive and negative mode, low and high collision energy) into an embedding, and a decoder pretrained on about 135 million molecules turns that embedding into SMILES strings. It is modelled on speech-to-text systems.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The decoder comes from a SMILES autoencoder with GRU encoder and decoder, pretrained on about 135 million PubChem and ZINC-12 molecules to translate between molecular representations. The spectra encoder is trained to predict that autoencoder's embedding from four spectra per compound: [M+H]+ and [M-H]- precursors at 35% and 130% NCE. Structures are produced either directly, by sampling several SMILES from the decoder and keeping valid ones, or indirectly, by retrieving database structures close to the embedding.
sections.source_locator: Paper Methods; README.md

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository holds one trained spectra encoder (spectra_encoder.pt) and the decoder model, vocabulary and config (decoder/models/), plus sample spectra and a sample embedding file. The encoder was trained on the NIST Tandem Mass Spectral Library 2020, a commercial dataset. A result should state whether the direct or indirect strategy was used and, for MassSpecGym, how the four-spectrum input was formed.

profile.summary: MetageNN assigns long sequencing reads to a genus. It does not align the read against a database: it counts short k-mers, 6-mers in the published setup, and feeds that profile to a neural network. The reason for using short k-mers is that they survive the high error rate of nanopore reads, which lets the model be trained on clean reference genome fragments and still work on noisy reads. Long reads are cut into 1 kbp chunks and the chunk predictions are combined by majority vote.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Results, Methods; README.md: opening paragraph, Counting k-mers

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Training sequences of fixed length, 1 kbp in the published work, are sampled from reference genomes. Each sequence is turned into a profile of canonical 6-mer counts with the Phylopythia k-mer counting tool, and that vector is the model input: the settings file for the main database gives a k-mer dimension of 6144 and a layer width of 3000, trained for 500 epochs at a learning rate of 0.001 with class weighting and a batch size of 1024. At prediction time a long read is split into non-overlapping 1 kbp chunks, each chunk is classified, and a majority vote decides the read's genus, with ties broken by the highest mean probability and predictions below a probability of 0.5 left unclassified.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Counting k-mers, Settings; settings/MetageNN_settings_main_database.json; Paper: Methods, Results

sections.title: Databases and training
sections.body: Two reference sets are used. The small database holds 47 genomes, from which about 235,000 sequences of 1 kbp were sampled at 1x coverage for the fine-tuning experiments. The main database expands that about ten times by randomly adding RefSeq representative genomes, giving 516 genomes across 505 species and 311 genera; the model for it was trained at 8x coverage with validation on 200 sequences per genome, and its capacity was roughly doubled in neurons per layer. The paper reports about 17 million samples in that training set, four GPUs and convergence by early stopping after three days.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository is a training setup, not a packaged classifier: it holds one training script, two settings files (small and main database), the genome and isolate lists, and a Google Drive link for the small database 1x training set. No trained weights are published, and the README says the preprint is still to be released, while the published paper exists. What a result must name is the database, the coverage, the k-mer length and the settings file, since those are what differ between the two configurations; the k-mer counting command and the vocabulary dimension have to match each other.

strengths.text: Short k-mer profiles are the point: they are less affected by sequencing errors, so a model trained on clean genome fragments transfers to noisy long reads without long-read training data.

The authors report it as small and fast against the tools they compared: less than a quarter of the database storage of Kraken2, MEGAN-LR and MMseqs2, more than 7 times faster than MetaMaps and GeNet. These are their own figures.

The authors report better sensitivity when the reference database is incomplete, which is the case that matters for novel lineages, and they test it with reads from species deliberately left out of the database.

profile.summary: ICEBERG predicts the tandem mass spectrum (MS/MS) of a molecule by simulating how it breaks apart in collision-induced dissociation. Given a molecular structure, collision energy and polarity, it generates plausible fragments and predicts their intensities, giving a spectrum. Its main use is ranking candidate structures for an unknown spectrum by how well their simulated spectra match.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: ICEBERG has two stages. ICEBERG-Generate builds a pruned fragmentation graph (a DAG) by learning which atoms break off, allowing up to three atom-breaking steps and six bond breakages; its training labels come from the MAGMa algorithm, which enumerates fragmentations and matches them to observed peaks. ICEBERG-Score takes the fragment graph, uses a GNN with instrument parameters to embed fragments and the parent molecule, and a set transformer to predict fragment intensities, which are merged into a spectrum. Version 2.0 added collision energy and polarity as inputs, contrastive fine-tuning and charge migration.
sections.source_locator: ICEBERG 2.0 preprint: Results and Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: ICEBERG 1.0 (Goldman et al., arXiv 2304.13136) is archived on the iceberg_1.0 branch; ICEBERG 2.0 (Wang et al. 2025) is on the iceberg_2.0 branch; the main branch holds ICEBERG 2.1, which the README calls about three times faster with official NIST'23 support, alongside the newer GLACIER model. Open MassSpecGym-trained ICEBERG 2.1 weights (msg_all and msg_simulation) are shared on Dropbox; NIST-trained weights are given only to NIST licence holders on request. ICEBERG 1.0 was evaluated on NPLIB1 and NIST20. A result should name the ICEBERG version and the training data of the weights.

sections.title: Use in the benchmark source

It also reports ICEBERG forward-model retrieval on the full MassSpecGym test split, imputing missing collision energies, and says MassSpecGym v1.5 releases officially retrained data-safe versions of ICEBERG and other components.

profile.summary: GeNet classifies shotgun metagenomic reads from raw DNA, without a similarity search against a reference database. It is a convolutional network: the bases of a read are embedded along with their positions, a ResNet style encoder reads them, and the output layers predict several taxonomic ranks at once, each rank's prediction able to see the one above it. The authors also use the network as a feature extractor, reporting that a linear model on top of its representations works for pathogen detection.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; README.md: opening paragraph; code/network.py: embeddings, build_conv_encoder

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A read is turned into two embeddings, one for the base and one for its position, over a vocabulary of six symbols, and a one hot encoding is also built. A convolutional encoder follows, made of ResNet blocks that downsample when the block changes and double the filter count, with the number of blocks, the filter count and the filter size set by command line flags. The taxonomy is the part that distinguishes the method: the output has one group of units per rank and, with connect_softmax set, the softmax activations of the higher rank are fed into the next, so the hierarchy between labels is used during training. Class weights per rank are applied through a one hot mask over the units of that rank.
sections.source_locator: code/network.py: embeddings, resnet_block, build_conv_encoder, weights; code/genet_train.py: flags and Config; arXiv abstract

sections.title: Training configuration and data
sections.body: The defaults in the training script are one ResNet block, 128 filters in the first convolution, a filter size of 3 in the row dimension, 1024 fully connected units, a batch size of 64, a read length of 10000, an initial learning rate of 1.0 and a simulated quality score of 15. The flag help gives the acceptance probability as 10 to the power minus the score over ten, while the code computes one minus that value. The configuration also fixes a vocabulary of 6 and an output vocabulary of 100. The repository ships the NCBI taxonomy nodes file and three id lists, for the training microbes, the full set and a pathogen set, and the README says the first run downloads the required genomes from NCBI.

profile.summary: CPA (Compositional Perturbation Autoencoder) is a deep generative model that predicts how single cells respond to drugs and genetic perturbations, alone or in combination. It is trained on a perturbation dataset of single-cell expression with perturbation, dose and covariate labels, and predicts expression for unseen combinations of perturbations, doses and cell types, with interpretable perturbation and covariate embeddings.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper Abstract and synopsis; README.md: What is CPA?

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: An encoder network decomposes each cell's expression into additive latent embeddings for its basal state, the observed perturbations and the observed covariates. An adversarial discriminator is trained against the encoder so the basal state carries no perturbation or covariate information, which lets embeddings be recombined at prediction time. Perturbation embeddings are scaled by a neural network of the dose or time. A decoder maps the recombined latent state back to expression.
sections.source_locator: Paper Results and Methods

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: CPA learns from a given single-cell perturbation dataset; the README's preprocessing recipe prepares the user's own dataset for it. The current implementation is the cpa-tools package in theislab/cpa, whose hyperparameter tuner is based on the scvi-tools optimiser; datasets and pre-trained models are in a Google Drive folder linked from the README. The paper's analyses are in a separate reproducibility repository. A result should name the package version or commit, the training dataset and the hyperparameters.

profile.summary: scRM (the single-cell read model) embeds single cells directly from raw sequencing reads, without a reference genome, gene annotation, count matrix or gene vocabulary. It takes paired 10x Chromium polyA FASTQ files, assembles each captured molecule from its reads, and learns a cell embedding from the base sequences; count matrices are used only as evaluation targets.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: A Rust pipeline reads paired FASTQ files, trims R2, corrects cell barcodes against the CellRanger called-cell list, deduplicates UMIs without any gene partition, and assembles one consensus sequence per UMI (one captured mRNA) with a de Bruijn graph at k = 19. The molecules are written to an Arrow corpus sorted by cell and packed into windows of 16384 tokens. The Python model is hierarchical (bytes, contig, UMI, window, cell): a byte-level local transformer trunk, attention pooling at each level, and a global trunk over UMI slots, both LLaMA-style pre-norm stacks. Training combines masked base modelling, EMA-teacher terms at UMI and cell level, and a SIGReg regulariser.
sections.source_locator: README.md: Architecture

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Three training arms are declared: S96, the flagship with global and local width 96, and S96ML and S96MA, mean-pooling ablations. The flagship recipe is fixed in code (arm S96, the corpora mouse_brain_5k, neuron_1k_v3, neurons_5k and sod1_spinal_cord, lambda 0.0196, seed 20260903, 8947 steps, 3000 training cells). Window length moves only on a ladder of 16384, 32768 and 49152 tokens, and runs at different rungs are different experiments. Checkpoints record the architecture hash and the regulariser. The sources do not offer a pretrained scRM checkpoint for download; the README's evaluation reads a checkpoint produced by training. A result should name the run, the arm, the seq_len rung and the commit.

sections.title: Intended uses
sections.body: Reference-free cell embeddings from raw reads (the paper's cross-species panels use rhesus monkey and rat corpora for training), scored against count-based controls and count foundation-model baselines on held-out datasets.

profile.summary: ProtCell is a foundation model for single-cell proteomics, where assays such as CITE-seq and CyTOF measure different, limited protein panels. It takes a cell's protein abundance profile over whatever panel was measured and learns cell- and protein-level representations, used for cell annotation, batch integration, imputing unmeasured proteins and choosing compact protein panels.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each measured protein is represented by a protein-identity embedding from a shared protein codebook plus a continuous embedding of its abundance. A transformer encoder (in the CUDA configuration: 8 layers, model width 256, 8 heads, feed-forward size 2048) is pre-trained by masking abundances (masked ratio 0.15) and reconstructing them with a mean squared error loss; a CLS token feeds the decoder. Inputs are CITE-seq data normalised by CLR or CyTOF data with ARCSIN preprocessing.

profile.summary: PLM-GraphDTA keeps the drug side of GraphDTA, a graph neural network over the molecule, and replaces its protein encoder with a fixed embedding taken from a protein language model. One vector per protein is computed in advance, projected by a small stack of linear layers, concatenated with the drug vector and sent through dense layers to one affinity value. It is the code behind a study comparing many protein embedding types, so the embedding source is a command line choice rather than part of the model.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The drug is a molecular graph with 78 features per atom, encoded by one of four GraphDTA style networks, here GIN, GAT, GAT_GCN or GCN, pooled by summation and projected to a 128 wide vector. The protein is not read as a sequence at all: a precomputed embedding, one vector per protein, is loaded from a json file and passed through linear layers with batch normalisation and ReLU, whose widths are set by the plm_layers argument. The two vectors are concatenated and sent through dense layers of 1024 and 256 units to a single output, trained with mean squared error and Adam. The input width of the protein branch is read from the embedding file itself, so changing the embedding type changes the first layer.
sections.source_locator: models/plm_ginconv.py: PLM_GINConvNet; training.py: embedding loading, optimiser

sections.title: Protein embeddings and splits
sections.body: The protein_embedding_type argument lists the embeddings the study compares: esm_320, esm_640, esm_1280, esmc_960, esmc_1152, deepfri_bp, deepfri_cc, deepfri_ec, deepfri_mf and prost_1024, with the number being the embedding width. The ESM script in the repository loads esm2_t30_150M_UR50D, takes the last layer's token representations and averages them over the residues to give one vector per protein. The repository also ships the fold files for several split regimes: setting1, drug_cold_1 to 5, protein_cold_1 to 5 and fully_blind_1 to 5, for the davis, davis_mutation and kiba datasets.
sections.source_locator: training.py: argument parser; preprocessing/ESM/esm_preprocessing.py; git tree listing: data folds

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There is one code release and no published weights. The repository has no README and no licence file, and the GitHub API returns a null licence field. What a result must name is therefore the run configuration: the model (PLM_GINConvNet, PLM_GATNet, PLM_GAT_GCN, PLM_GCNNet, and the plain GraphDTA and ESM_GATNet baselines the script also imports), the dataset, the embedding type, the plm_layers widths, the fold setting and the seed. Seeding is implemented: with a seed given, the script sets deterministic algorithms and turns cudnn benchmarking off. Training runs 1000 epochs at batch size 512 and saves the model at the best training loss, then evaluates that model on the held out fold.

facts.label: Model type
facts.value: Supervised drug-target affinity regression model: a GraphDTA drug encoder with a frozen protein language model embedding as the protein representation.
facts.source_locator: models/plm_ginconv.py: header, PLM_GINConvNet; GitHub API response: description

facts.label: Architecture
facts.value: Five GIN convolution layers of width 32 over the drug graph (or the GAT, GAT_GCN or GCN variant), sum pooling to a 128 wide vector; a protein branch of linear layers with batch normalisation over the precomputed embedding, default width 128; concatenation, then dense layers of 1024 and 256 units to one output.
facts.source_locator: models/plm_ginconv.py: PLM_GINConvNet; git tree listing: models

facts.label: Inputs
facts.value: A drug molecular graph with 78 node features, and one precomputed embedding vector per protein, read from a json file such as proteins_esm_320.json. The protein sequence itself is not fed to the model.

strengths.text: The protein representation is a plug: ten embedding types are selectable on the command line, from three ESM-2 widths through ESM Cambrian and DeepFRI function embeddings to ProstT5, and the model reads its input width from the embedding file.
Hard splits are shipped, not just a random one: drug cold, protein cold and fully blind folds for both datasets, five of each.
strengths.source_locator: training.py: argument parser; git tree listing: data folds

strengths.text: Runs can be made deterministic: given a seed, the script seeds python, numpy and torch, sets the cublas workspace, turns cudnn benchmarking off and asks torch for deterministic algorithms.
The plain GraphDTA models are in the same codebase and the same training loop, so the comparison between a learned sequence encoder and a language model embedding is made under one harness.
strengths.source_locator: training.py: model imports; git tree listing: models

limitations.text: There is no README and no documentation in the repository, so every command has to be reconstructed from the argument parser.
limitations.source_locator: git tree listing; training.py: argument parser

limitations.text: The checkpoint is selected on training loss, not on a validation split: the script saves whenever the training loss improves, then evaluates that saved model on the test fold.
No licence is declared for the code or the shipped data, so reuse terms are unclear.

It needs a GPU and a prior embedding pass. The training script uses CUDA mixed precision and 24 data loader workers by default, and the protein embeddings must be computed first with a separate script for each embedding type.

diagram.title: PLM-GraphDTA workflow
steps: protein sequences are embedded once by a protein language model and averaged over residues
the per protein vectors are stored in a json file
the drug graph is encoded by a GIN, GAT, GAT_GCN or GCN network
the protein vector passes through linear layers set by plm_layers
the two vectors are concatenated and sent through dense layers
output: one affinity value, scored by RMSE, MSE, Pearson, Spearman and CI
diagram.caption: The language model runs before training, not inside it, so the affinity model only ever sees one vector per protein.

The reported results, the embedding comparison and which configuration the authors recommend are not described here.
The ESM Cambrian, DeepFRI and ProstT5 preprocessing scripts in the repository were not read, so only the ESM-2 embedding route is described.
No licence is declared, so whether the shipped Davis and KIBA copies may be redistributed is not established.

run_guide.summary: Compute the ESM-2 protein embeddings for a dataset, then train and evaluate one PLM-GraphDTA variant on it.
prerequisites: The repository gives no environment file, so the dependencies have to be read from the imports: torch with CUDA, torch_geometric, fair-esm, rdkit, networkx, pandas, numpy, tqdm and wandb.
A CUDA GPU. The training script uses mixed precision through torch.cuda.amp and the embedding script moves the language model to the GPU when one is present.
No data download: the Davis and KIBA drug, protein and fold files are in the repository.
No licence is declared for the code or the shipped data.

steps.title: Get the code at the pinned commit
steps.shell:
git clone https://github.com/matija-marijan/PLM-GraphDTA.git
cd PLM-GraphDTA
git checkout --detach 53b9428a0f48bdcf2a863682b7185957e23c8fb1
steps.explanation: The repository has no README, so these lines are added here to get the code at the commit these notes were read at. The address is the repository the GitHub API response describes as the source code for PLM-GraphDTA.
steps.source_locator: GitHub API response: html_url, description; git tree listing: sha

steps.title: Compute the protein embeddings
steps.shell: python preprocessing/ESM/esm_preprocessing.py
steps.explanation: The script loops over the davis, kiba and davis_mutation datasets, embeds each protein with esm2_t30_150M_UR50D, averages the last layer over the residues and writes data/<dataset>/proteins_esm_<width>.json. The file name carries the embedding width, which is what the training argument then refers to. The script takes no arguments in the version read.

steps.title: Train and evaluate one configuration
steps.shell: python training.py --dataset davis --model PLM_GINConvNet --protein_embedding_type esm_640 --plm_layers 128 --fold_setting setting1 --seed 42 --cuda 0
steps.explanation: The flags are the ones training.py's argument parser defines, with values from the help strings: a dataset name, a model from the table in the script, an embedding type, the widths of the protein branch, a fold setting and a seed. The embedding type must match a proteins_<type>.json file produced by the previous step, so set it to the width that step printed.
steps.source_locator: training.py: argument parser, model table, embedding loading

steps.title: Or run a plain GraphDTA baseline for comparison
steps.shell: python training.py --dataset davis --model GINConvNet --fold_setting drug_cold_1 --seed 42 --cuda 0
steps.explanation: Leaving out the embedding type runs one of the plain GraphDTA models in the same loop, with the default embedding width of 128 that the script sets when no precomputed embeddings are used.

outputs: Protein embedding files under data/<dataset>/, one json per embedding type.
A checkpoint and a results csv under trained_models/testing/, named after the run configuration.
Test set metrics printed at the end: RMSE, MSE, Pearson, Spearman and CI, and written into the results csv.
Optional Weights and Biases logging when --wandb is passed.

lit-interactions-20261011-plmdta-model-p.notes: This record's existing source, the Marijan and Tanasijevic 2026 preprint (doi 10.64898/2026.08.31.748056), is the study this repository belongs to: the repository description names the same title. The preprint is bioRxiv only (pdf at https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.08.31.748056v1.full.pdf) and was not fetched in this pass, so the page is written from the code alone and coverage is limited. Two things a reviewer may want to check against the preprint: the training script selects its checkpoint on training loss rather than a validation split, and the ESM preprocessing script as committed uses esm2_t30_150M_UR50D with two larger models commented out, while the training argument offers esm_320, esm_640 and esm_1280 widths. The repository also contains an esm_gat model and ESM Cambrian, DeepFRI and ProstT5 preprocessing scripts that were not read. Sibling record DeepGraphDTA from the same preprint has no file of that name in this repository and was left as a stub.
